query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of chromium to boride‐based components will promote the in situ formation of a protective chromium‐rich oxide scale during hot‐dip aluminum plating, thereby reducing molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard boride-based component (without additional doping) used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low concentration of chromium (e.g., by surface alloying or diffusion treatment) into the boride-based component.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied such that during typical hot-dip aluminum-plating processes (at temperatures around 660°C) the chromium can oxidize and form a continuous protective scale. The intervention assumes controlled processing that yields an optimal chromium level (roughly 1–3 wt.% locally) without altering the bulk properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, continuous chromium-rich oxide layer at the surface/interface of the boride component.
generation.mechanism: The chromium in the doped layer preferentially oxidizes during exposure to high-temperature molten aluminum, forming a stable Cr-oxide that acts as a diffusion barrier. This barrier limits the penetration and direct interaction of molten aluminum with the boride matrix, thereby suppressing corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped boride components, chromium-doped components will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate, improved surface integrity, and less elemental interdiffusion at the metal–moltens aluminum interface during hot-dip plating.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without chromium doping, which typically develop unprotected surfaces that allow for more rapid molten aluminum attack and corrosion.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions. If the chromium doping is too low (insufficient to form a continuous oxide) or too high (potentially altering other material properties), or if the process parameters do not facilitate oxide scale formation, the intervention might not be effective.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement and the optimal chromium concentration are uncertain and will require further quantitative electrochemical and microstructural studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based components: one set doped with a trace amount of chromium (in the target 1–3 wt.% range) and a control set without chromium. Subject both sets to molten aluminum immersion tests at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (≈660°C) for identical durations. Characterize the samples before and after exposure using microscopic imaging (SEM), compositional analysis (EDS), and weight-loss measurements.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional SEM imaging to assess oxide scale continuity and thickness.
EDS or XPS to confirm the presence and distribution of chromium and its oxide.
Weight loss or corrosion depth measurements to quantify corrosion rate differences.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the chromium-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher corrosion rates, poor oxide scale formation, or no measurable barrier effect) compared to the undoped control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Selective Laser Melting (SLM) Additively Manufactured CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy: Process Optimization, Microscale Mechanical Mechanism, and High-Cycle Fatigue Behavior

Abstract: AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) possesses excellent properties including exceptional strength–ductility synergy, high corrosion resistance, and good thermal stability. Selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing facilitates the convenient fabrication of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA parts with complex geometries. Here, the SLM process optimization was conducted to achieve a high relative density of as-built CoCrFeNiMn HEA bulks. The mechanisms of process-induced defects and process control were elucidated. The microscale mechanical behaviors were analyzed through in situ scanning electron microscopy observation during the compression tests on micro-pillars of the as-built HEA. The stress–strain characteristics by repeated slip and mechanism of “dislocation avalanche” during the compression of micro-pillars were discussed.
